title: Cadillac reveal special livery for Las Vegas Grand Prix
excerpt:
Cadillac have become the latest team to showcase a bespoke livery that will feature on their car for the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Nov 17, 2026 5:39pm UTC

Cadillac have revealed a unique livery that will feature on the team’s car for the Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend, the American outfit’s final home event of the season.

Alongside the MAC-26’s usual colour scheme, the design features a translucent-look effect that the squad have said offers a “look beneath the surface”, adding that the livery is “a tribute to the ingenuity, innovation and countless unseen efforts that have brought our debut season to life”.

It comes as Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas prepare to take to the Las Vegas Strip Circuit for Cadillac’s maiden outing at the track, with the team still searching for their first points of the campaign.

The squad have joined the likes of Williams and Aston Martin in showcasing special designs for this weekend’s event.

title: Audi announce Felbermayr for third F1 ACADEMY season in 2027
excerpt:
Audi have confirmed that Emma Felbermayr will contest a third F1 ACADEMY season next year, with the Austrian driver remaining part of the Audi Driver Development Programme.

The 19-year-old made her single-seater debut in 2025, taking her maiden victory in the all-female series in Montreal alongside a campaign in Spanish F4.

This season, Felbermayr launched herself into title contention, achieving a Feature Race victory in Shanghai alongside podium finishes in China, Montreal and Silverstone. She currently sits third in the Standings heading into the season finale in Las Vegas.

Felbermayr will remain with Rodin Motorsport for her third campaign, with the Audi junior permitted to return following a rule change announced last year, which is available to drivers whose performance indicates strong potential for continued growth.

Speaking on the announcement, Allan McNish, Director of the Audi Driver Development Programme, said: "We are pleased that Emma will continue representing us in F1 ACADEMY in 2027. Since making the step into single-seaters, she has shown considerable progress, and her performances this year have further confirmed her potential.

“We know she has the speed and determination to compete at the top of the grid, and we believe there is still more to come from her. Supporting young talent and giving drivers the right environment to develop is at the heart of the Audi Driver Development Programme: we are very much looking forward to continuing our work with Emma and Rodin Motorsport next year."

Felbermayr continued: "I am very happy to be continuing with Audi Revolut F1 Team and Rodin Motorsport for another season in F1 ACADEMY. I have learned so much over the past two years, both on and off the track, and I am very grateful for the trust and support they have shown me.

“We have enjoyed some great moments together, and I feel I have made a lot of progress as a driver, especially this season, but I also know there is still plenty I can improve. Having the chance to return for a third season means a lot to me, and I am really looking forward to working with everyone again and seeing what we can achieve together in 2027."

Benn Huntingford, Sporting Director of Rodin Motorsport, added: “We are pleased to welcome back Emma for the 2027 season. She has continued to demonstrate great potential and we look forward to supporting her development, fighting at the front of the grid.”

title: Sainz on his 250th GP and Williams’ ‘most important year’
excerpt:
Over 11 years on from his first appearance in Formula 1, Carlos Sainz is preparing to mark his 250th race start at the Las Vegas Grand Prix. Ahead of the milestone, the Spaniard sat down with F1.com to reflect back on the key moments of his journey so far, how he bounced back from the challenges, and why 2027 could be the “most important year” of Williams’ project…

It is two weeks before Sainz reaches his landmark number of races when we catch up on the topic in Williams’ hospitality during a busy media day at Interlagos. Some drivers might feel a sense of retrospection about the impending event – but for Sainz it appears that this isn’t necessarily the case.

“No, honestly, just a level of pride in the fact that F1 is a very tough sport to have a lengthy career,” he explains.

“And just the fact I'm reaching the milestone of 250, still at 32 years of age, is something that makes me feel proud of myself, of the team around me, of the way my career is going. [I’m] going to try and keep going [for] another 250 from here.”

A competitive start and getting McLaren onto an ‘upward spiral’

While he might be firmly looking forward, Sainz admits that he can still recall the feelings at play when he was preparing to line up on the Formula 1 grid for the first time at the 2015 Australian Grand Prix, having been given his debut with the then-called Toro Rosso team.

“I definitely remember the nerves of that first week in Australia,” he says of that event, in which he would go on to score his maiden points with a P9 finish. “From Monday I was just looking forward to practice and asking myself how quick will I be finally with others on track, and [to] see myself on the timesheets and where will I be?

“And I remember straight after FP1, I had a very competitive weekend in general and that just gave me a massive boost of confidence and saying, 'Okay, I belong here'. The fact that I was so quick in lower categories means I can also be quick in F1, and the first week in F1 just taught me that I'm ready for this.

“The big difference is that I didn't have as much testing as the rookies have nowadays, like I was not given any FP1s, any tests, so I had a lot more question marks going into the weekend.”

After nearly three seasons with the squad, Sainz moved to Renault towards the end of 2017 before switching to McLaren for the 2019 campaign, forming an all-new line-up alongside rookie Lando Norris.

It would prove to be a memorable two-year spell for the Spanish racer, who scored his maiden podium at Sao Paulo in 2019 as well as taking a second rostrum one year on at Monza.

Pushed on whether he views this time as a pivotal moment in his career, Sainz responds: “I think that McLaren is seen as a pivotal moment because I had three very strong years in Toro Rosso but then I had a bit of a difficult year in Renault, and then the contrast between my year in Renault with such two great years in McLaren makes it look like a pivotal moment.

“But I actually think my first three years in Toro Rosso were almost as good as my two years in McLaren, so it's just that gap year in Renault where, I don't know why, I didn't find a good feeling with the team, with the car, and the contrast between Renault to McLaren was so big that it looked like a pivotal year, but it was pivotal also because we achieved the first podiums for McLaren in a long time.

“We managed to change that team around a lot and we managed to gather a lot of momentum in that team, and it went from being a bit of a downward spiral to suddenly, with my arrival and Lando's, we turned it into an upward spiral and upward momentum.”

From a special first win to how Ferrari exit ‘ignited a fire’

The next big step came for Sainz in 2021 when he replaced Sebastian Vettel at Ferrari. After promptly collecting four podiums during his first season with the team, the Spaniard later achieved perhaps his biggest milestones so far in one weekend during the 2022 season.

On his 150th start, Sainz took pole position at the British Grand Prix and subsequently converted this into his maiden victory during a thrilling race.

When assessing how this feat compares to the three wins he has gone on to achieve since, the 32-year-old admits that holding a unique relationship with Silverstone made his first triumph even more special.

“I think that win stands out in the fact that it was the first one,” he says. “I think if you tell me of the quality of the wins and the weekends that I did, probably Singapore [2023], Australia [2024] and Mexico [2024] are higher quality weekends. But the fact that I won at Silverstone…

“I did my first pole position in the wet, which I've always loved the wet driving and always been very quick at Silverstone, and actually my first-ever single-seater pole position was at Silverstone. My first-ever race win in a single-seater was at Silverstone.

“Coincidentally my first-ever pole position in Formula 1 was at Silverstone, and my first-ever race win in Formula 1 was at Silverstone, so that track is extremely special and the fact that I achieved it there for me just meant I had some kind of special bond with that track and with those fans that just made me feel very, very special.”

Despite his run of success with the Scuderia, Sainz was faced with perhaps his toughest curveball to date when he learned prior to the 2024 campaign that he would be departing the team at the end of the season following their signing of Lewis Hamilton – a sequence of events that would prove difficult but, as Sainz explains, ultimately motivating.

“It was definitely one of the most challenging moments of my career, if not the most challenging, because it was one of the times that I've performed at my highest level in Formula 1,” Sainz concedes.

“I think [during] that beginning of 2024, I was performing at a very high level, also towards the end of 2023 and with my win in Singapore, so it was completely unexpected. It came completely out of the blue.

If anything, [being dropped by Ferrari] ignited a fire in me that made me have one of my strongest seasons in Formula 1.Carlos Sainz

“The fact that I kept thinking I was just going to renew my contract and keep going for many more years with Ferrari, to all of a sudden being dropped and having to concede the seat to Lewis.

“But if anything that ignited a fire in me that made me have one of my strongest seasons in Formula 1, and I think I put together a very strong campaign – two very special wins in Australia and Mexico that year, a very solid year in general, and it did almost good to me mentality-wise and approach-wise.”

Enjoying his Williams arrival and why 2026 is a ‘gap year’

Sainz took the time to contemplate his options after learning of his impending departure from Ferrari. After being linked to numerous teams, the four-time Grand Prix winner ultimately signed a multi-year deal to race for Williams from 2025 onwards – making him one of a select number of drivers to have gotten behind the wheel for the sport’s three most historic teams, McLaren, Ferrari and Williams.

The first campaign together would prove to be more fruitful than perhaps many would have imagined – given the tough 2024 season that the Grove-based outfit had endured – with Sainz claiming the team’s first podiums since 2021 in Azerbaijan and Qatar.

“For sure, the history of the team and the fact that Williams has been such a successful team in Formula 1 added to the fact of taking the decision to come to Williams,” the Spaniard says. “But the reality is that I came to Williams, apart from that, mainly for performance, because I thought there is performance in this team and there is evolution to be had.

“And that first year, bringing the team back to the podiums, scoring three podiums – two in the normal races, one in the Sprint [at the United States Grand Prix] – kind of proved my point of when I come to Williams to make it successful again and big again.

“I really enjoyed last year – it's probably [the case that] those podiums are the podiums that I've actually enjoyed the most in my career in Formula 1 because of what they meant to me. Unfortunately this year we're going through a bit of a very, very tricky situation, but I still believe that we can turn it around.”

The 2026 season was indeed challenging from the off for Williams, the outfit immediately finding themselves on the back foot after missing the Barcelona Shakedown before starting the campaign with an overweight car. Points have been sparse, leaving them in P9 of the Teams’ Championship on a tally of 12 – seven of which have been scored by Sainz.

Amid the squad slipping backwards from the highs of last year, Sainz and team mate Alex Albon have been praised by Team Principal James Vowles for the supportive manner in which they reacted to the problems. Does Sainz feel that the experience he has gathered over his nearly 250 races has helped him to deal with the issues?

Why Sainz has put his faith in Williams once again

“A hundred per cent,” he acknowledges. “I don't think I could have dealt with this the way I've dealt with it this year eight years ago, let's say, or five years ago even.

“I think perspective and experience give you a level of understanding and analysis that, when I analyse my current situation and the fact that I'm not even fighting for the points in any races this year, has allowed me to sit philosophically and say it's a gap year.

“As long as I still perform and I still maximise what I have in the car and in the team, and I'm still helping this team to develop and improve, it can still be considered a good year, while before I used to be a lot more results-driven and I would have been maybe scared of people thinking that I'm not anymore fighting for the top or anything.

“But now I am very comfortable, let's say, in my own skin on what I am doing, the way I'm working with the team, the way I'm achieving the results and maximising the performance, and definitely having a solid year in terms of performance has helped the fact that I've not fought for any big things this year.”

Celebrating the 250th and the ‘biggest target’ for Williams in 2027

The 2027 season will be an important one for Williams in terms of their history, with the team preparing to mark their 50th anniversary year in Formula 1 – and Sainz admits that the campaign is also particularly crucial in terms of the squad’s on-track performance.

“Being completely honest, I think next year is Williams' most important year of our project,” he says. “We need to prove to everyone that we can turn it around. We need to prove it to ourselves. This year has been a bit of a gap year, and I don't think the team can really afford another year like this one.

“If we're really wanting to show to everyone that we're being serious and we're really wanting to get this team back to the top, it needs reaction from a bad year, and I see a team working flat-out in order to achieve this.

“I've put all my energy and all my efforts into making sure it doesn't happen again with whatever I can control within my feedback, factory and simulator sessions, etc.

“It's going to be an important year, but if you ask me personally, I do think the team have taken a lot of steps this year in order to correct all the mistakes that we've done, and there's been huge change, huge transformation inside the team to make sure it doesn't happen again, so I have trust that it will not, considering how important it is.”

The team have taken a lot of steps this year in order to correct all the mistakes that we've done.Carlos Sainz

In the shorter term, Sainz’s next focus will be on his milestone 250th race at the Las Vegas Grand Prix. When asked if he has any celebrations planned – such as a special helmet design – the Spaniard smiles: “No, but you just give me the idea that probably I should do something!

“I'm not a very statistical guy – I don't look at statistics much. The fact that my first win was in the 150th and Vegas is going to be my 250th does make me want to do something special and, maybe now that you've told me only two weeks before the race, I will try and make something happen!”

Pushed on what his hopes and targets are for what comes next – and where he would like to be by the next milestone, his 300th Grand Prix – Sainz has some clear goals in mind.

“By the time of the 300th that will be another 50 races, which is approximately two seasons,” he reflects. “By then I would have liked to take Williams back on the podium and get Williams back in the top five in the Constructors' [Championship], knocking on the door of the top four.

“I think if we manage to do that in the next 50 races that would be huge progress from where we are today, which is very far, so that's my biggest milestone. That is my biggest target over the next 50 – but I'm hoping that that's only 50 of the next many more.”

title: Williams retain Jade Jacquet for 2027 F1 ACADEMY campaign
excerpt:
Williams have announced that Jade Jacquet will continue to represent the team for a second F1 ACADEMY season, with the French driver remaining with ART Grand Prix in 2027.

The 16-year-old heads into the final round of her rookie campaign in Las Vegas riding the high of her most successful weekend yet in the all-female series, having scored her first points alongside achieving a best finish of P4 in the Austin Feature race.

Jacquet also made history earlier this year when she became the first female to win a French F4 race, having also taken multiple top 20 finishes.

Looking to build on the foundations she’s made during her first season, Jacquet will remain as part of the Williams F1 Team Driver Academy, and she expressed her delight at the opportunity to return for another campaign.

“I’m really pleased to be continuing my journey in F1 ACADEMY with the Williams F1 Team Driver Academy,” she said. “I’ve loved being part of Williams and ART Grand Prix this past year, and I can’t wait to start my second season in F1 ACADEMY, taking everything I’ve learned from my rookie season and applying those skills into 2027.

“I’ve grown a lot over this season, and I feel Austin, with my P4 finish and first points, is just the beginning for me. I’m proud to be part of the Williams F1 Team Driver Academy and pleased to be lining up on the F1 ACADEMY grid with Williams and ART again next year.”

Sven Smeets, Sporting Director at Williams, added: "I’m delighted that Jade and Williams will continue our journey together in 2027 along with ART Grand Prix. She has progressed significantly this season, growing in confidence with every race, and Austin was a real highlight. We’re pleased to keep supporting her development through the Williams F1 Team Driver Academy next year, and I’m looking forward to seeing what she can achieve.”

title: How the Sphere became the heart of the Las Vegas GP
excerpt:
From giant driver portraits to live onboard footage and race updates, the Sphere has become one of the defining sights of the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Having opened just weeks before Formula 1 returned to the city in 2023, the enormous entertainment venue quickly became part of the race's identity, with its illuminated exterior providing a spectacular backdrop to the action.

But the Sphere is far more than a giant advertising screen. With its ability to display everything from yellow flags to live footage, its become a staple of the race with increasingly creative ways to showcase information.

What is the Sphere?

The Sphere opened on September 29, 2023, with Irish rock band U2 beginning a 40-show residency at the venue. Its distinctive design and enormous LED exterior immediately made it one of Las Vegas' most recognisable landmarks.

Made up of 54,000 metres squared of LED displays on its exterior, it is the largest video screen in the world, and inside, an audience of up to 20,000 people are treated to a 16K resolution wraparound interior LED screen.

Formula 1 returned to Las Vegas on November 18, 2023, more than four decades after the city hosted the Caesars Palace Grand Prix in 1981 and 1982. With the Sphere sitting alongside the new circuit, it quickly became part of the event's identity, entertaining fans while providing live updates from the track.

How F1 embraced the Sphere

Right from the off, the Sphere would sync with the FIA’s circuit calls, displaying a huge yellow flag and a wrap-around Safety Car message, or a rippling red flag if the session had come to a stop.

Orbi, the giant yellow emoji face displayed on the Sphere, even donned a racing helmet and appeared to watch the cars as they exited Turn 9. Driver profiles were also on a loop, helping educate fans about what the drivers looked like outside of the cockpit and which teams they drove for.

And since then, the use of the huge display that measures 112m high and 157m wide has got ever more creative. Onboards were a frequent feature during the 2025 event, showing the cars lapping this rapid 6.201km track layout.

"The Sphere has become a great partner, and so we have a lot of advanced conversations and meetings to organise the different types of content,” Austin Brown, VP of Marketing at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, explains.

"We have the partnerships content as well as chequered flags, yellow and red flags, and then we have some podium celebrations, so it's a combination of F1's broadcast team cueing content in real time with the Sphere team who are on site for the duration of the week.

"We actually pull some of the telemetry data from the feed that goes over to the Sphere team, so that we can track things like fastest lap; depending on how the race results end up, we can post that content live to Sphere. So we pre-build a lot of the content that's driver- or team related, and some of these moments that we know might occur on track, and then we feed that data or the broadcast team cues live content to align with track activity for broadcast, socials or the on-site experience with fans in attendance.”

Where sport, entertainment and technology mix

The Las Vegas Grand Prix has proved to be the pinnacle of F1’s entertainment ecosystem, with continuous celebrity spotting, big shows and performances across the race weekend, and definitely follows the saying “everything is bigger in Vegas”. For the race organisers, the Sphere was going to be no exception.

“Las Vegas' role on the F1 calendar is to push the sports and entertainment landscape,” Brown says, describing the Sphere as “an iconic canvas” that is “a massive win for everybody involved".

As a Las Vegas native, Brown loves to see the tourist attractions showcased on the Sphere, and adds that the vibrancy of its neon colours fits a night race very well.

"To see a lot of the F1 drivers at that scale on Sphere is just a really fun opportunity. We've pre-filmed content with drivers in the past where they're taking different actions on the Sphere; there's an opportunity for animated and still graphics up there. To see Lewis Hamilton at the scale of Sphere is just a really special moment to deliver to fans. We're excited to see what kind of content is produced and live this year.”

Bringing the Las Vegas experience to F1

Inside the Sphere, the schedule is packed. After this year’s Las Vegas Grand Prix, Backstreet Boys will be performing the Official Afterparty at Sphere. They’re one of several groups and artists who have had residencies at the unique venue, with others including the likes of Metallica and No Doubt, and more are scheduled throughout 2027, with John Mayer and P!nk both booked in.

As well as pop royalty, there are also many immersive shows to watch inside such as The Wizard of Oz which comes with 4D effects. The grand space of the venue, which can fit the entire Statue of Liberty inside, has 17,385 seats and uses Stereographic Projection and custom cameras to capture the ultra-wide videos and images that you see on the wraparound screens.

“I think when Liberty Media acquired the sport, and then F1 was looking at new markets back in 2022, that is when they really started to explore Vegas as a market,” Brown concludes. “I think it was really trying to find a platform to continue to grow the sport to a lot of untapped fans in the US. So where better to do that than in the sports and entertainment capital of the world with a night race that just shows off everything the city has to offer?

“We've worked really hard to try and deliver what the city offers in the way of entertainment, food, beverage, and hospitality, and pull that onto track so that it's one cohesive Vegas experience."

What began as an eye-catching backdrop to F1's return to Las Vegas has become something much more. Three years on, the Sphere is firmly established as part of the Grand Prix experience, bringing the action on track to life on a scale unlike anywhere else on the calendar.

title: Brown on why McLaren struggled to fight for title in 2026
excerpt:
McLaren CEO Zak Brown has given his take on the reasons why the team struggled to challenge for the championship in 2026 – but the American was also keen to avoid an “excuse”, adding that the squad have “just got to do a better job”.

The 2024 season saw the papaya outfit score their first constructors’ title since 1998 – and while Max Verstappen took the drivers’ crown on that occasion, McLaren clinched both championships in 2025 with Lando Norris claiming his maiden triumph.

Amid the introduction of sweeping new technical regulations for the 2026 season, the team were overtaken by rivals including Mercedes and Ferrari as the campaign got underway.

Signs of progress emerged later in the season – with Norris taking back-to-back victories in Hungary and the Netherlands before more recently winning again in Sao Paulo – but McLaren remain in fourth place of the teams’ standings on a 17-point deficit to third-placed Red Bull.

During an appearance on Sky Sports' The F1 Show, Brown was quizzed on whether there was an impact into 2026 from the fact that the team were developing their 2025 car late into that season.

“What’s great is we kind of never talk about it, because we don’t want to have excuses,” Brown responded. “But, reality is you get the least amount of wind tunnel time because the team that won gets it – but we never kind of talk about that.

“We were developing and racing pretty hard last year up to the last race. Some teams went, ‘We’re done for ’25, let’s focus on ’26.’ And then also, not being a works team, when a new technology comes out, there’s a lag of understanding how everything works.

“So if I think about how we know the power unit works today versus Australia, night and day, and the works team – rightfully so – they get a head start on you because they’re the works team.

“We’ve now kind of caught up, maybe not yet to their level of knowledge, but we’ve come a long way. So when you kind of package that all together… but what I never want that to make it sound like is an excuse. We’ve just got to do a better job.”

With this in mind, Brown admitted that there are plenty of learnings that the team will take forward from the MCL40 for their 2027 challenger.

"Weight was a big issue this year for a lot of cars, obviously a shorter wheelbase [results in a] lighter car,” he explained.

"So yeah, I think there's things that… Slow speed corners weren't great for us. We've learned a lot about the power unit this year, and deployment, and all the stuff that we're all still learning.

"I think this season, there's a lot of takeaways and changes we're going to make going into 2027."

title: Alonso set for Dakar Rally return with Aston Martin
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso will compete in the Dakar Rally for Aston Martin in January 2027, marking his return to the event after seven years.

Alonso is set to drive the Aston Martin Dreadnought as part of a three-car challenge alongside nine-time World Rally Champion Sebastien Loeb and reigning World Rally Raid Champion Lucas Moraes.

The Spaniard will be joined by co-driver Marc Coma, a five-time Dakar motorcycle category winner who sat alongside Alonso during his 2020 debut in the event – in which he finished 13th overall.

With the 2027 Dakar taking place in the Sahara Desert between January 9 and 23 – beginning in Portugal and then racing through Morocco – Alonso will then turn his focus to the 2027 F1 season, with pre-season testing scheduled for February before the campaign gets underway in March.

"After deciding to continue racing in Formula 1 with the Aston Martin Aramco, I thought carefully about Dakar," said Alonso. "In the end, the decision became simple. I wanted to embrace the challenge completely and take on both Formula 1 and the Dakar Rally in the same year.

"In 2020, Dakar was one of the most challenging and enjoyable experiences of my career. I have enormous respect for this race and the specialists who have mastered it. Having Marc alongside me again is very important, and with Aston Martin, Prodrive, Sebastien and Lucas we have an exceptional team.

"Formula 1 remains my priority. But I am a racing driver, and challenges like this are why I love competing. I’m looking forward to seeing what we can achieve."

Alonso’s previous participation in the Dakar Rally occurred during his two-year hiatus from Formula 1 between 2019 and 2020, with the Spaniard also taking part in other feats such as the Indianapolis 500 as well as winning the World Endurance Championship.

title: Aston Martin showcase bespoke Las Vegas Grand Prix livery
excerpt:
Aston Martin have become the latest team to unveil a special livery for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, a collaboration with their Official Cloud Compute Partner CoreWeave.

Featuring shades of white and black alongside the team’s signature green, an announcement revealing the design states that the look was “inspired by the two organisation's shared ambition to Pioneer the Possible”, adding that it “celebrates CoreWeave's integration into the team, from the AMR Technology Campus to each race weekend”.

As well as adorning the AMR26, the design will also feature across the team’s garage and Lance Stroll's helmet during the event.

Jefferson Slack, Managing Director, Commercial and Marketing, Aston Martin Aramco, said: "The Las Vegas Grand Prix gives us a fantastic opportunity to showcase the strength of our collaboration with CoreWeave through this unique livery takeover. What makes this collaboration particularly exciting is the work happening behind the scenes.

"From helping our engineers make sense of race communications in near real time to identifying new directions in aerodynamic development, we're seeing how CoreWeave can change the way we operate.

"This is about more than technology for technology's sake. It's about giving our people the tools to challenge assumptions, discover new opportunities and keep pushing the boundaries of what's possible."

The livery reveals follows on from Williams’ unveiling of their own one-off design for Las Vegas.

title: Sergio Perez makes bold prediction once Cadillac fixes car issues
excerpt:
Sergio Pérez believes Cadillac will soon start "over-delivering" once the team closes the performance gap to the midfield in F1.

Pérez and team-mate Valtteri Bottas have endured a difficult campaign with the new American outfit, which has so far failed to score a point over the 20 grands prix. Its best result has been Bottas' 13th in the second race of the season in China.

Pérez, who has finished a high of 14th on three occasions, has pointed to his own performances as proof the driving side of the equation is not the issue.

"We have said it before; the level that I've been driving at this year has been really top, getting the maximum out of the car in very difficult conditions, on very difficult occasions," he said, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365.

"We're not lacking anything on the driver side. Once we get a little bit more performance, once we close the gap a little bit more to the midfield, we will start.

"I'm pretty confident we will be over-delivering. The thing is, we are over-delivering a lot as a team, but the car is still too far away. Once we get it a little bit closer in the races, we will be making very good show-offs."

[Article continues below]

Cadillac frustrations

The 36-year-old also addressed why Cadillac's breakthrough has taken so long to materialise, pointing to the financial and operational restrictions that come with building a new team from scratch.

"Just putting everything, all of the puzzle together, with the [various] departments, before we see a real impact in car performance," he said.

"Everything in Formula 1 takes too much time, unfortunately. You are very limited with things that you can change quickly, with the budget cap and with the people you can get in place and so on, so that hasn't been a fairly easy thing for the team."

The team has recently brought in senior aerodynamic and design personnel in an effort to address the car's underlying concept, though the full effect of that restructuring is unlikely to show until next year's design cycle.

title: Liam Lawson draws on 'one thing' he can boast about after Red Bull stint
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has stated he has proven he can be competitive at Red Bull following his stint with the team earlier this year.

The New Zealander was called up to replace Isack Hadjar when the latter suffered an injury during the summer break.

Lawson scored two top-seven finishes in the three rounds he was behind the wheel, a sizeable improvement on his form at the start of 2025, when he lasted just two rounds before being demoted back to Racing Bulls.

Having had a more positive run the second time around, Lawson maintains that he did not get a fair shot when he was promoted for the first time.

"There was a lot of talk over the last 12 months after I left Red Bull that maybe I wasn't a driver good enough to drive for Red Bull because of my start," Lawson told media including RacingNews365.

"It's not something I've spoken too much about, but going back to the start of 2025, we did half a day in Jerez before the season, we had a compromised Bahrain test, missed FP3 in Melbourne with an engine issue, and China was a sprint.

"That was it. Versus this year, I felt like I've seen a lot more experience going into Red Bull this year.

"If there's one thing I take from it, it's that at least I can show people that I can drive that car, or any car."

[Article continues below]

Lawson highlights challenge of Red Bull stint

Lawson was in the middle of a strong campaign with Racing Bulls when he was called up to replace Hadjar at the senior team in August.

He was forced to alter all he knew about how to prepare for a race weekend due to the differences at Red Bull, resulting in a challenging few events behind the wheel.

"It was very tough,” he reflected. “Your whole process, you come from a team where you do the same thing every weekend.

"Then you go to another team during the season and you have to adjust a lot.

"It was a very focused, intense few weeks. Personally, I don't think it hurt me. It was interesting to get a different perspective on the car as well.

"Over the years, I've driven a lot of different stuff. I still haven't completed a full season with the same team, but it helps with your adaptability."

title: How Zak Brown turned McLaren from disaster into a £3 billion empire
excerpt:
This weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix will represent 10 years since Zak Brown joined McLaren, overseeing a dramatic recovery to the top of Formula 1 from practically the bottom.

Zak Brown will mark 10 years in charge at McLaren this weekend in Las Vegas, a milestone that bookends one of the most dramatic turnarounds in modern Formula 1.

Brown joined as executive director of McLaren Technology Group in November 2016, stepping into the void left by Ron Dennis's departure from operational leadership.

He was officially elevated to chief executive officer in April 2018, inheriting a team ravaged by boardroom instability and a crumbling Honda partnership.

The Honda years had been brutal. McLaren's tightly packaged "size zero" engine bay left no room for a competitive power unit, and reliability and performance suffered badly. Aerodynamic correlation issues with the team's wind tunnel went undetected until the switch to customer Renault power in 2018 exposed just how far McLaren had fallen behind.

Brown's response was structural as much as sporting. He oversaw the end of the James Key era as technical director, replacing a single figurehead with a three-pronged technical structure under Peter Prodromou, Neil Houldy and later Rob Marshall, while promoting Andrea Stella to team principal after Andreas Seidl's exit.

That division of labour, Brown with commercial strategy, Stella with racing operations, has since been credited by Brown himself as central to the team's cultural stability.

Investment followed. McLaren commissioned its own wind tunnel and composite manufacturing facility at Woking, ending reliance on an external Toyota facility in Cologne, and brought a modern driving simulator online at the McLaren Technology Centre.

The highs, the lows, and the controversial moments

The on-track results have followed too. Lando Norris claimed McLaren's first drivers' title since 2008 last season, while Oscar Piastri was a genuine title contender of his own.

The team sits fourth in this year's constructors' standings, though its 2024 and 2025 championship-winning form has made the season's drop-off a visible comparison point.

Not every chapter has been smooth. Brown's 2022 letter to the FIA accusing Red Bull of cheating over its cost-cap breach drew accusations of grandstanding from rivals.

The team's equal-opportunity "papaya rules" policy between Norris and Piastri has repeatedly been questioned by paddock observers as a risk to a genuine title campaign, a debate Brown has insisted will continue into 2026.

More recently, McLaren's legal battle with Alex Palou and Chip Ganassi Racing over a breached IndyCar contract ended in an early 2026 settlement after a High Court ruling.

Commercially, the transformation has been just as stark. McLaren's ownership has shifted from MSP Sports Capital's minority stake at a £560 million valuation in 2020 to a buyout by McLaren Group, backed by Bahrain's Mumtalakat and Abu Dhabi's CYVN Holdings, now valued above £3 billion.

Brown has also expanded the sponsor roster past 50 partners, landing deals with Google, DP World and Mastercard along the way.

Ten years on, the papaya outfit that once scrapped for scraps at the back of the grid now arrives in Las Vegas fighting at the front.

title: George Russell delivers insight into plan to topple Kimi Antonelli
excerpt:
George Russell missed out on a maiden F1 title this year, with team-mate Kimi Antonelli taking the crown instead.

George Russell has hinted at how he plans to rejuvenate himself and take the fight to team-mate Kimi Antonelli going forward.

Antonelli won his maiden F1 title this year in just his second season in the sport, becoming the youngest champion in F1 history.

While Russell suffered his share of reliability woes, the Briton was consistently outpaced by Antonelli across the campaign.

Russell is now in a fight for second place in the standings and is facing stiff competition from several drivers to secure the runner-up spot.

As he targets a boost in form for 2027, Russell stated he will continue to use a sports psychologist, having done so for several years.

"I've been working with sports psychologists for seven years now, and these were through my most successful years in Formula 1," he said.

"Now, of course, this has been the first year of real struggle.

"At least in the approach I have, we're not boxers where you're in a ring fighting directly against somebody else.

"We're kind of fighting against ourselves, almost like a golfer."

Driver

George Russell

British

63

Russell explains 'like a golfer' comparison

Russell explained that the best approach for him is to focus on his own performance, rather than finding weaknesses in his opponents.

Having enjoyed a run of strong seasons prior to the 2026 campaign, Russell insisted he is keen to discover how he can recapture the elements that made him deliver impressive performances in previous years.

"A qualifying lap, you're there by yourself, and it's the work and preparation that you've done yourself that makes the difference between a good performance and a bad one," he said.

"So, I'm not directly looking at my number one competitor, saying, 'How am I going to beat this guy?'

"I'm more looking at myself in the mirror, thinking, 'What do I need to do to not have these poor performances? What were the feelings I had from myself and the car during the great performances, so I can replicate that more often?'"

title: Mercedes to unleash long-awaited F1 upgrade at Las Vegas GP with a twist
excerpt:
Mercedes will have a fresh upgrade in its arsenal this weekend at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Mercedes has confirmed that it will bring its ADUO upgrade to the Las Vegas Grand Prix this weekend.

The ADUO scheme, which stands for Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities, was introduced by the FIA this year to let power unit manufacturers trailing the performance benchmark bring forward otherwise frozen homologated updates.

Mercedes qualified for the concession after its internal combustion engine was found to be two to four per cent off the pace set by the Red Bull Ford Powertrains unit, which topped the FIA's review.

That banding meant Mercedes was granted only one upgrade this season and one in 2027, fewer than manufacturers assessed as more than four per cent behind.

After a delay to its introduction, team boss Toto Wolff has now confirmed that it will be in use in Las Vegas this weekend - but only on Kimi Antonelli's car.

"We will have the ADUO enabled turbo specification available from this weekend," Wolff said.

"This is primarily about proving out the development in race-weekend conditions, with the expected performance benefit relatively small.

"We anticipate running it with Kimi, whilst with George our priority is protecting his grid position with the performance benefit likely too limited to justify taking a grid penalty."

[Article continues below]

Wolff hails F1 over Middle East events decision

The introduction of the upgrade comes at the start of the final triple header to round out the season, with trips to Qatar and Abu Dhabi following the round in Las Vegas.

The journey to the Middle East comes after a long period of scrutiny over whether or not the events would go ahead due to the tension in the area.

With the rounds now confirmed to be on, Wolff commended F1 for the work it has done behind the scenes.

"After Vegas, we're looking forward to heading to the Middle East for Qatar and Abu Dhabi," he said.

"A lot of work has gone on behind the scenes, and credit should go to Formula One and the FIA for ensuring we can complete the season as planned.

"We always enjoy racing in the region and receive incredible support there.

"The two circuits present very different challenges, so there is plenty for us to learn, and we're excited to finish the year in front of those fans."

title: Argentina F1 return 'rumour' revealed after significant Rwanda announcement
excerpt:
Franco Colapinto believes Formula 1's newly confirmed African Grand Prix does not diminish Argentina's own chances of returning to the calendar, with the Alpine driver revealing he has heard rumours of F1 wanting to be back in Argentina before the Rwandan race's scheduled early-2030s debut.

Formula 1 announced a 10-year agreement last month to stage a grand prix in Rwanda, on a purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, roughly 40 kilometres south of Kigali.

The deal marks the sport's first return to the African continent since 1993 and follows the collapse of earlier talks to revive the South African Grand Prix at Kyalami.

The news has reignited questions over Argentina's own long-standing push to rejoin the calendar, a campaign that has gathered momentum on the back of Colapinto's rise through the sport.

Argentine officials have held exploratory talks with F1 and the FIA over a potential race at the Autódromo Oscar y Juan Gálvez in Buenos Aires, though the circuit still requires significant investment to meet FIA Grade 1 standards.

[Article continues below]

Franco Colapinto confidence remains in Argentina F1 return

Asked whether Argentina's hopes had been hurt by the Rwanda announcement, Colapinto told media including RacingNews365 that he saw it as a positive step for the sport rather than a setback for his home country.

"First of all, going to Africa, I think it's a very good thing for the sport to include new countries, new continents, to include a different part of the world," said Colapinto.

"It's going to be a good thing for the sport, and we saw it in the past. We need tracks, we need races, new places to go to. Malaysia was a super positive race.

“I think going back to a track that is so enjoyable for the drivers is something very special, and again, going to Rwanda is going to be amazing. So I am looking forward to it.

"I think Argentina has the same amount of probability as before; that hasn't really changed. Also, having Rwanda in 2030, it's still a long time away. I think Argentina is for a bit earlier, from what I hear from the rumours.

"So hopefully, if it happens, we can go everywhere. But not very many more races, you know," Colapinto joked.

title: Zak Brown issues ‘BS’ stance as McLaren anniversary nears: ‘Just not welcome’
excerpt:
Zak Brown has outlined the zero-tolerance approach that has underpinned his decade in charge of McLaren's commercial and leadership operations, insisting that honesty, not excuses, is what he demands from those around him.

The comments arrive ahead of this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, with Brown marking 10 years since taking up his role at the team.

McLaren head into the Las Vegas round sitting fourth in the constructors' championship on 398 points, with three wins to their name so far this season, as they continue to build on the foundations Brown has overseen since joining McLaren in late 2016 before becoming McLaren Racing CEO in 2018.

Among the defining calls of that tenure was elevating Andrea Stella to team principal, a decision Brown says had been on his mind long before it actually happened.

Speaking on the Sky F1 podcast, Brown said he feels McLaren now has exactly the group of people he wants around him.

"I definitely feel like I have my dream team," he said. "Andrea [Stella], I wanted him to do the job the first time around, and he felt he wasn't ready yet. So maybe I kind of was a little bit visionary, and actually, Andrea, I think you're going to make a great team principal. But the first time around, he felt he wasn't ready. Second time around, he felt ready."

"I love tough decisions because a lot of people don't, and I think the role as the CEO is kind of the buck stops with you, and so I have to make those decisions. So you have to get used to leaning in, and, you know, it doesn't mean that's always fun, depending on what the decision is."

"But I like making tough decisions, and I have very low tolerance. I've got a lot of time for mistakes. I put up my hand. Let me do something differently. Let me learn from that. No problem. B.S. That's just not welcome. Own it. I've made a tonne of mistakes."

McLaren's change of approach in signing Lando Norris

Brown also pointed to the signing of Lando Norris as a defining moment in McLaren's turnaround, describing it as a departure from the team's traditional approach.

"I'm so proud of how we responded," Brown said.

"Responded by bringing in Lando, that was, other than Lewis, this is a team that's historically gone for the proven multi-world champion, and that was a risk. Putting Andrea in charge, my whole leadership team."

"I think our secret sauce, and we all talk about culture, but all the credit for that really sits with my leadership team and how they've run their kind of independent businesses. But, more importantly, how we all come to work together."

title: Max Verstappen response to hilarious Red Bull radio: 'He doesn't speak English'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen might have won best radio message of 2026 in Brazil.

Max Verstappen had everyone laughing on Friday in Brazil with a team radio message about his engine. The Dutchman has since explained exactly what the problem was, joking his car "doesn't speak English".

The award for team radio of the 2026 season may already have been decided. On Friday at the São Paulo Grand Prix, the four-time world champion aired his frustrations over the clutch and engine braking on the RB22 by appearing to have a conversation with his own power unit.

Red Bull ultimately swapped the engine after the session, resulting in a grid penalty for Verstappen which saw him start in 21st before recovering to second.

Speaking to Viaplay, Verstappen looked back on the moment, explaining what exactly had gone wrong on board his car.

The Red Bull driver started off joking about the radio message before turning serious on the subject.

"I think he doesn't speak English," Verstappen laughed, when asked about talking to his engine.

"I'm still trying to figure out what language he does speak. I haven't tried Dutch yet; I don't know. He didn't respond very well..."

title: Lewis Hamilton stripped of podium as Ferrari suffer intra-team collision - On This Day
excerpt:
The 2019 Brazilian Grand Prix was an absolutely crazy one! Penalties and intra-team clashes, it had it all.

Seven years ago today, Max Verstappen claimed one of the most dramatic wins of his career at Interlagos, as both Ferraris crashed out of the 2019 Brazilian Grand Prix and Lewis Hamilton was stripped of a podium finish by the stewards.

Verstappen converted pole position into victory, leading home Pierre Gasly and Carlos Sainz in a result few had predicted before the chequered flag.

Gasly, starting sixth for Toro Rosso, crossed the line 6.077 seconds behind the Red Bull driver to claim what remains the finest result of his career, while Sainz completed the podium for McLaren despite starting a lowly 20th on the grid, following a late engine change.

The result was shaped as much by misfortune for others as by the pace of the front-runners. Sebastian Vettel and Charles Leclerc, who had qualified second and fourth respectively, collided with six laps remaining while fighting over what was then third place.

Leclerc had gone around the outside of his team-mate into Turn 1, only for Vettel to find a tow down the Reta Oposta and drift into his path.

The contact broke Leclerc's right-front suspension and punctured Vettel's rear tyre, ending both cars' races on the spot.

The stewards investigated the clash after the race but opted not to take further action, ruling that both drivers had contributed to the incident and had each had a chance to avoid it.

Ferrari team principal Mattia Binotto summoned Vettel and Leclerc to Maranello in the aftermath, stating that responsibility for the crash was shared between the pair.

According to The Guardian, the team subsequently made clear that while its drivers remained free to race each other, prioritising the team's interests and avoiding on-track collisions was non-negotiable going forward.

Lewis Hamilton, who had started third, also saw his race unravel. On the penultimate lap, following a late restart, the Mercedes driver attempted a move around the outside of Alex Albon at Turn 10 for what was then second place.

The pair made contact, spinning Albon around and ending his afternoon. The stewards judged that Albon had been on the racing line and that Hamilton was predominantly to blame for attempting the move into a closing gap, handing him a five-second penalty and two penalty points on his licence.

The penalty dropped Hamilton from an on-track third to an eventual seventh in the final classification.

The Interlagos clash between the Ferrari drivers was later described as the culmination of mounting tension between Vettel and Leclerc that year over status within the team, a rivalry that would help shape Ferrari's direction for seasons to come, with Leclerc eventually handed a long-term extension and Vettel's Maranello career drawing to a close not long after.

title: Bernie Ecclestone criticises Ferrari's Italian 'politics' over latest title failure
excerpt:
Bernie Ecclestone has spoken out on his thoughts on Ferrari this season.

Bernie Ecclestone has claimed that Ferrari should have won this year's world championship, while suggesting team principal Fred Vasseur is overwhelmed by the job.

The former Formula 1 supremo made the comments to RTL/Sky Sports as Ferrari's 2026 campaign heads towards its conclusion still without a title.

Mercedes has run away with both championships this season, with Kimi Antonelli sitting top of the drivers' standings on 390 points after 20 rounds, well clear of Max Verstappen on 279.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton sit fifth and fourth respectively, with the Scuderia 142 points adrift of Mercedes in the constructors' table.

Ecclestone, who has long been a vocal critic of Ferrari's internal politics, argued the Maranello outfit possessed the fastest car on the grid this year but was let down by its own structure.

"Ferrari should have won the world championship this year," Ecclestone insisted. "They had the best car. So many different things went wrong.

"I've been saying for many years, ever since I convinced them to bring in a Frenchman as team principal: there are too many Italians.

"Everyone thinks they know better how to run the team, that it's being run incorrectly, and that they could do it better."

Fred Vasseur 'overwhelmed' by Ferrari leadership position

Ecclestone went further, turning his attention directly to Vasseur, who has led Ferrari since the start of the 2023 season.

"To be honest, he's a nice person, but simply overwhelmed by the task of running a team like Ferrari," added Ecclestone.

"Ferrari needs a very, very, very strong person who thinks about Ferrari from the moment they wake up until they go to sleep. [...] I wonder if he really devotes the majority of his thoughts to Ferrari."

The remarks arrive despite Vasseur and senior Ferrari management having previously pushed back on rumours of leadership instability, insisting that stability and working in calm conditions were what the team needed to succeed.

Vasseur himself has conceded that Ferrari knew from the season opener that its power unit was down on output compared to Mercedes and Red Bull, a deficit he said severely limited the team's title prospects despite a strong chassis.

Leclerc has echoed that technical explanation, pointing to a straight-line speed shortfall relative to Mercedes and Red Bull as the car's main handicap, while insisting Ferrari's wind tunnel correlation with on-track performance remained positive.

Whether that power unit deficit can be resolved for 2027, and whether Vasseur will be given further scope to restructure the team beneath him, remain open questions heading into the winter.

title: Ferrari replace Lewis Hamilton for Las Vegas GP first practice
excerpt:
Ferrari has confirmed that Dino Beganovic will replace Lewis Hamilton for first practice at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, fulfilling the final mandatory rookie session of Ferrari's 2026 campaign.

The Scuderia has now completed all four of its required rookie outings for the season.

Beganovic has already deputised for Hamilton in Spain and for Charles Leclerc in both Austria and Brazil, meaning this Las Vegas appearance closes out Ferrari's obligations under the expanded rookie rule.

Formula 1's sporting regulations, broadened from 2025, require every team to hand FP1 duties to a rookie, defined as a driver with no more than two grand prix starts, across at least two sessions per car each season.

That adds up to four mandatory FP1 appearances per team over the year.

The Las Vegas Strip Circuit is not typically viewed as a forgiving venue for rookie running. Unforgiving concrete walls, low initial grip and a track surface that evolves sharply from a green first practice to a heavily rubbered, cooler nocturnal session make set-up work unrepresentative, and teams have generally been reluctant to hand such a session to an inexperienced driver.

Ferrari, however, had little choice given the timing of its remaining commitment. Beganovic, a Ferrari Academy member since 2020, has built up FP1 mileage across the year and was recently confirmed to be stepping up into a full-time reserve and development role with the Scuderia from 2027.

He will not be the only reserve on duty in Las Vegas. Haas has also opted to field Ryo Hirakawa in FP1, standing in for Oliver Bearman as it too works through its rookie-running requirements before the season concludes.

title: McLaren striving to make 'peace' with Las Vegas after persistent struggles
excerpt:
McLaren boss Andrea Stella is optimistic heading into the Las Vegas Grand Prix, where he hopes the team can vanquish its Sin City demon.

Andrea Stella hopes McLaren can finally make "peace" with the Las Vegas Grand Prix this weekend, with recent upgrades offering encouragement ahead of a return to one of the team's most troublesome circuits.

The Woking-based squad has endured three difficult visits to Nevada, culminating in last year's double disqualification for excessive skid wear.

While Lando Norris' victory in São Paulo provided a timely boost, the long straights of the Las Vegas Strip Circuit will place different demands on the MCL40.

McLaren's shorter gear ratios have contributed to its limitations at circuits where outright top speed is particularly important. The lengthy flat-out section along the Strip therefore threatens to expose a weakness already evident at Monza and Baku.

Stella acknowledged that the layout presents a challenge as McLaren seeks to carry its improved form into the weekend.

"It's a very different circuit layout, Vegas, long straights," Stella told media, including RacingNews365.

"We have seen this in Monza; we have seen this in Baku: when the requirement is to develop top speed, McLaren is not necessarily the best car.

"We know that this also somehow relates to our gear ratios that are not ideal when you need to go above a certain level of top speed."

[Article continues below]

Upgrades offer McLaren hope

McLaren introduced a new front wing in Brazil to improve the car's predictability and driveability, with further parts due in Las Vegas.

Those developments also form part of its preparations for 2027, giving the team reasons for encouragement beyond Norris' Interlagos victory. Stella believes the lessons from Brazil can help McLaren extract more from its package in Nevada.

"But having said that, I think we approach Vegas with some optimism because the car is faster now," Stella added.

"I think this race will give us, and not only us, but everyone, I think, a bit of understanding of how to use the tyres, and where the car is good, where their car or our car is less good. So there's information to be capitalised on for Vegas as well."

[Article continues below]

Three years of frustration

Both McLarens exited Q1 in 2023, before Norris crashed after bottoming out. Oscar Piastri finished P10.

In 2024, tyre graining, understeer and a loss of aerodynamic efficiency when reducing rear-wing downforce contributed to Norris and Piastri finishing sixth and seventh.

Last year brought a stronger performance, with Norris taking pole before finishing second and Piastri fourth. However, both were disqualified after their rear skid blocks fell below the minimum permitted thickness. McLaren attributed the excessive wear to unexpected porpoising, which increased contact with the track.

"So, we look with some optimism, and also Vegas is... we want to go there and have a good result because it's probably been, of all the races on the calendar, the one that we've been struggling the most at," Stella said.

"And even last year, when we had a good race, we made our life bad with the problem that we had with the skid.

"So we look forward to Vegas, have a good result there, and finally be at peace with this venue."

title: Exclusive: Formula E chairman planning multi-company event extravaganza
excerpt:
Formula E chairman and co-founder Alejandro Agag is planning on a multi-company event extravaganza in 2028, holding the all-electric single-seater series and his electric powerboat series E1 on the same weekend at the same location.

Agag, who co-founded Formula E, founded two other all-electric categories. He founded the off-road Extreme E - now known as Extreme H - in 2021 and, most recently, E1 in 2024.

It had been planned for Monaco to host Formula E and E1 on the same weekend this year, although the Principality was against the idea of having two events on the same dates, preferring to stage them separately.

However, that only reignited talks of having Formula E and E1 take place on the same weekend at the same place, demonstrating the advancement of electric mobility on land and water.

Formula E and E1’s calendar both feature three of the same destinations: Monaco, Miami and Jeddah.

RacingNews365 understands Miami and Jeddah are the two most probable options for it to happen, with Monaco having declined hosting both on the same weekend this year.

The idea is for the events to take place on the same day at different times, allowing eyeballs to bounce from one to the other.

2028 joint event target

The problem with Miami, though, is both events taking place in very different locations. Formula E races at the Miami International Autodrome, while E1 is at Biscayne Bay 25 kilometres away.

From a different perspective, Jeddah is the most logical, with Formula E at the Jeddah Corniche Circuit and E1 at the Obhur North waterfront being just 13 kilometres from one another and both along the Red Sea.

"So we're really trying to make that happen," Agag exclusively told RacingNews365 in Miami at the E1 finale.

"We were actually trying to do it in Monaco this year, but Monaco prefers to have the event separately, I guess because maybe hotels and, like, this, they have two events. But it would be great to have both at the same time.

"So, potentially, Miami is one option. I mean, there are many options because we have places where we race that have the scenery. Tokyo, for example, could be incredible for having Formula E and E1 together.

"So, yeah, definitely, I think soon we will have a joint Formula E and E1 event."

The idea of both on the same weekend in the same city is currently being explored for as soon as 2028, with Agag hungry to turn the idea into a reality.

"We've been trying to do it next year," added Agag. "I think it's going to be 2028. We will coordinate the calendar with Formula E and try to make it happen in 2028."
